title: The identity crisis of speciation genomics
content:
Abstract
Understanding how reproductive isolation (RI) evolves remains a central goal of speciation research. Quantifying RI is challenging, and researchers can rely on either organismal proxies (e.g. hybrid fertility or fitness) or genetic proxies (e.g. gene flow or genomic divergence). The increasing availability of genomic data has transformed the field, enabling inference of genomic divergence and patterns of gene flow across diverse taxa. As a result, speciation research has become increasingly dominated by genomic approaches. Here, we combine a literature survey with a reanalysis of publicly available datasets to evaluate the consequences of this dominance. We show that genetic data and concepts have become increasingly dominant in inferring RI, yet genetic proxies can be unreliable, as genomic divergence does not consistently predict the strength of reproductive barriers. We recognize that this imbalance is not without justification: genetic proxies can be applied across a broader range of taxa than organismal proxies, which often require controlled crosses or fitness assays that are logistically demanding or simply infeasible in many systems. We conclude by recommending: (i) the distinction between studying the mechanisms underlying RI (speciation) and the patterns associated with speciation (diversification); (ii) a ‘back to basis’ approach, reinvigorating classic experimental designs, fieldwork, and population studies with genomic data; (iii) renewed tests of chromosomal models of speciation; and (iv) stronger links between estimates of gene flow and both intrinsic and extrinsic reproductive barriers.
